lessons.title: Openings and closings
lessons.tip: The first and last moments matter most. Open with something that wakes the audience up: a question, a short story or a surprising fact. Do not start with “Today I will talk about…” Close by returning to your main message and ending with a clear thought or call to action.
sources: Esenwein and Carnegie, The Art of Public Speaking (1915, public domain): delivery, openings and closings
Aristotle, Rhetoric, and Cicero’s five canons (public domain); Silva Rhetoricae (BYU) for device names (concepts only)

lessons.title: Signposts
lessons.tip: Signposts tell the audience where you are going, like road signs. At the start, give a map: “I have three points.” Between points say “My second point is…” At the end say “To sum up…” Signposts help listeners who cannot go back and re-read.
sources: Esenwein and Carnegie, The Art of Public Speaking (1915, public domain): delivery, openings and closings
Aristotle, Rhetoric, and Cicero’s five canons (public domain); Silva Rhetoricae (BYU) for device names (concepts only)

lessons.title: Repeat for rhythm
lessons.tip: A tricolon is a list of three: “Stop, look, listen.” Three feels complete and is easy to remember. Anaphora repeats the same words at the start of sentences: “We will work. We will learn. We will win.” Both build rhythm and make a line memorable.
sources: Esenwein and Carnegie, The Art of Public Speaking (1915, public domain): delivery, openings and closings
Aristotle, Rhetoric, and Cicero’s five canons (public domain); Silva Rhetoricae (BYU) for device names (concepts only)

lessons.title: Contrast and questions
lessons.tip: Antithesis puts opposite ideas side by side: “Easy to say, hard to do.” It makes a point clear and strong. A rhetorical question is asked for effect, not for an answer: “Who wouldn’t want a safer street?” It makes the audience think.
sources: Esenwein and Carnegie, The Art of Public Speaking (1915, public domain): delivery, openings and closings
Aristotle, Rhetoric, and Cicero’s five canons (public domain); Silva Rhetoricae (BYU) for device names (concepts only)

lessons.title: Pause and stress
lessons.tip: A pause is a tool. Pause before an important word to build attention, and after it to let it sink in. Stress the key word: “We need ACTION” means something different from “WE need action.” Short pauses also give you time to breathe and think.
sources: Esenwein and Carnegie, The Art of Public Speaking (1915, public domain): delivery, openings and closings
Aristotle, Rhetoric, and Cicero’s five canons (public domain); Silva Rhetoricae (BYU) for device names (concepts only)

lessons.title: Pace, volume and pitch
lessons.tip: Your voice has three controls: pace (speed), volume (loudness) and pitch (how high or low). A flat voice makes people drift away. Speak a little slower for important points and a little louder for key ideas, and let your pitch fall at the end of a statement to sound sure.
sources: Esenwein and Carnegie, The Art of Public Speaking (1915, public domain): delivery, openings and closings
Aristotle, Rhetoric, and Cicero’s five canons (public domain); Silva Rhetoricae (BYU) for device names (concepts only)

lessons.title: Body language
lessons.tip: Your body speaks too. Stand tall with your feet apart. Look at different people for two or three seconds each. Use open hands at chest height for gestures, and move with a purpose, not back and forth. Keep your hands out of your pockets.
sources: Esenwein and Carnegie, The Art of Public Speaking (1915, public domain): delivery, openings and closings
Aristotle, Rhetoric, and Cicero’s five canons (public domain); Silva Rhetoricae (BYU) for device names (concepts only)

lessons.title: Manage your nerves
lessons.tip: Nerves are normal: your body is getting ready. Turn the energy into focus. Slow your breathing: in for four, out for six. Know your first sentence by heart. Practice aloud, not only in your head. Remember that the audience wants you to do well.
sources: Esenwein and Carnegie, The Art of Public Speaking (1915, public domain): delivery, openings and closings
Aristotle, Rhetoric, and Cicero’s five canons (public domain); Silva Rhetoricae (BYU) for device names (concepts only)
